Majorization-Guided Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models under Modality-Specific Shift

CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligence
Lixian Chen Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, China email: 3123003175@mail2.gdut.edu.cn , Mingxuan Huang Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China email: huangmx53@mail2.sysu.edu.cn , Yanhui Chen Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, China email: chenyanhui91@mails.gdut.edu.cn , Junyi Lin Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, China email: 3123001378@mail2.gdut.edu.cn and Yang Shi Affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, China email: sudo.shiyang@gmail.com
Abstract.

Vision-language models transfer well in zero-shot settings, but at deployment the visual and textual branches often shift asymmetrically. Under this condition, entropy-based test-time adaptation can sharpen the fused posterior while increasing error, because an unreliable modality may still dominate fusion. We study this failure mode through a majorization view of multimodal posteriors and cast adaptation as a constrained de-mixing problem on the fused prediction. Based on this view, we propose MG-MTTA, which keeps the backbone frozen and updates only a lightweight gate or adapter. The objective combines fused-posterior entropy minimization with a reliability-aware gate prior built from anchor-based modality consistency and cross-modal conflict. Our analysis gives conditions under which entropy reduction preserves the correct ranking and a threshold that characterizes modality-dominance failure. On the ImageNet-based benchmark, MG-MTTA improves top-1 accuracy from 57.97 to 66.51 under semantics-preserving textual shift and from 21.68 to 26.27 under joint visual-textual shift, while remaining competitive in the visual-only benchmark. These results show that multimodal test-time adaptation should control modality reliability, not just prediction entropy.

Keywords: 
vision language model, test time adaptation, majorization, doubly stochastic mixing, modality specific shift

1. Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a standard foundation for multimodal recognition, retrieval, and open-vocabulary understanding. Their large-scale pretraining substantially improves zero-shot transfer and cross-modal reasoning across diverse tasks. However, realistic deployment rarely preserves the source-domain conditions seen during pretraining (Gu et al., 2023; Oh et al., 2023). Instead, the two modalities are often perturbed asymmetrically: the visual stream may suffer from blur, occlusion, low illumination, or style shift, while the textual stream may exhibit prompt-template drift, lexical variation, or other forms of semantics-preserving phrasing shift (Gu et al., 2023; Zhang and Tian, 2025; Sun et al., 2025). The resulting challenge is therefore not merely uncertainty under a single distribution shift, but multimodal decision-making under modality-specific shift.

This asymmetry creates a failure mode that is specific to multimodal fusion. When one modality becomes unreliable but remains artificially sharp, entropy minimization can further increase confidence in an incorrect fused decision (Yang et al., 2024). In other words, a lower-entropy posterior is not necessarily a better posterior once fusion is driven by modality imbalance. A satisfactory test-time adaptation method for VLMs should therefore do more than sharpen predictions: it should identify when entropy reduction corresponds to genuine recovery and when it merely amplifies the influence of a corrupted modality.

Our starting point is to view modality-specific shift through posterior geometry. We model each modality-level posterior as a doubly stochastic mixing of an underlying clean posterior, up to a residual that captures deviation from the idealized mixing model (Marshall et al., 2011). Under this view, test-time adaptation becomes a constrained de-mixing problem on the fused posterior. This perspective is useful for two reasons. First, it provides a principled explanation of why entropy may increase under shift and why a successful update should reverse that trend only along a valid majorization direction (Marshall et al., 2011; Sagawa, 2022). Second, it exposes the role of modality reliability in fusion: if one stream is poorly explained by the mixing model or conflicts sharply with the other stream, its contribution should be downweighted during adaptation (Zhang et al., 2023; Papandreou et al., 2009). Throughout the paper, we distinguish between an ideal analysis object based on doubly stochastic mixing and its practical implementation. The former clarifies the majorization geometry of multimodal degradation and recovery, whereas the latter is realized by a computable modality-to-anchor reliability proxy built from running anchors.

Based on this formulation, we propose a majorization-guided test-time adaptation method that keeps the vision-language backbone frozen and updates only a lightweight gate or adapter module. The method combines entropy minimization on the fused posterior with reliability-aware regularization derived from two computable signals: an anchor-based reliability proxy inspired by doubly stochastic fit, and a cross-modality disagreement proxy that reflects conflict between the two streams. The resulting objective keeps the trainable subset small and is directly aligned with the theoretical quantities used in our analysis.

We further show that entropy reduction is beneficial only under additional structural conditions. In particular, if the adapted fused posterior moves along a correct majorization direction and preserves the decisive ranking induced by the clean fused posterior, entropy reduction is accompanied by prediction preservation. Conversely, when the gate overweights a biased modality beyond an explicit threshold, the fused decision can be forced to flip. The empirical evaluation follows this separation. Visual corruption benchmarks provide a standard CLIP test-time adaptation anchor, while semantics-preserving textual shift and joint shift form the main multimodal evaluation. Conflicting textual perturbations, such as negation or class-inconsistent descriptions, are reserved for failure analysis because they probe modality dominance more directly.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We identify a multimodal-specific failure mode of entropy-based test-time adaptation under modality-specific shift, where lower entropy can reflect confidence amplification by a biased modality rather than genuine recovery.

  • •

    We formulate this problem as a multimodal posterior de-mixing problem based on majorization and doubly stochastic mixing, and derive conditions under which entropy reduction is beneficial together with a modality-dominance threshold that characterizes a concrete failure regime.

  • •

    We propose a lightweight adaptation method that updates only a gate or adapter module while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, using reliability-aware regularization based on an anchor-based reliability proxy and cross-modality disagreement.

  • •

    We establish an evaluation protocol that separates visual shift, semantics-preserving textual shift, and joint shift, while treating conflicting textual perturbations as failure analysis rather than as part of the main robustness benchmark.

2. Related Work

2.1. Test-Time Adaptation

Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt a source model to unlabeled target data at inference time without full retraining (Liang et al., 2024). Representative methods reduce predictive entropy, update normalization statistics, stabilize predictions with teacher models, filter unreliable samples, or restrict adaptation to small parameter subsets for robustness (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2023). These approaches have been especially effective in image classification, where the model output is usually treated as a single posterior to be sharpened or stabilized under shift.

The multimodal case is more delicate. Once prediction depends on both visual and textual streams, lower entropy does not by itself imply a better decision. The outcome also depends on whether fusion remains aligned with the more reliable modality. This difference motivates the setting considered here, where the visual posterior, the textual posterior, and the fused posterior are treated as separate but coupled objects.

2.2. Vision-Language Models under Shift and Test-Time Adaptation

Vision-language models built on contrastive pretraining and large-scale multimodal learning have substantially improved transfer across recognition, retrieval, and open-vocabulary tasks (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Alayrac et al., 2022). At the same time, their predictions remain sensitive to prompt design, visual corruptions, and broader distribution shift (Xiao et al., 2024; Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019; Oh et al., 2024). Existing studies have mainly documented this sensitivity through performance degradation, calibration, or prompt robustness analyses (Oh et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2023), making clear that robustness remains fragile once deployment conditions depart from pretraining.

Recent work has therefore extended TTA to vision-language and multimodal models through prompt tuning, lightweight adaptation, or reliability-aware correction (Shu et al., 2022a; Karmanov et al., 2024; Maharana et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). These methods are the closest practical neighbors to our setting because they adapt frozen or lightly updated multimodal backbones under target shift. Still, most existing formulations are organized around entropy minimization, consistency, or heuristic reliability adjustment. Although robustness is evaluated on the fused prediction, the fused posterior itself is usually not treated as the object of analysis. As a result, current methods say relatively little about when entropy reduction preserves the correct fused ranking and when it instead reinforces a biased modality. Our formulation focuses on this point directly by studying multimodal adaptation at the fused-posterior level.

2.3. Fusion, Reliability, and Majorization

A separate line of work studies multimodal fusion under modality imbalance and shows that reliability-aware weighting can improve prediction by reducing the influence of noisy or misaligned streams (Li and Tang, 2024; Sidheekh et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023). This line of research provides an important practical intuition for our setting: when the modalities are not equally trustworthy, robust fusion should not weight them equally.

Separately, majorization theory provides a natural language for describing how probability vectors become more mixed or less mixed (Marshall et al., 2011). While it is closely related to entropy and posterior geometry, it has rarely been used to study multimodal adaptation. In this paper, majorization is not used only as a descriptive tool. It is also used to clarify when entropy reduction corresponds to genuine recovery and when a sharper prediction is simply a sharper mistake under modality-specific shift.

3. Method

MG-MTTA adapts a frozen vision-language model by updating only a lightweight fusion module at test time. For each test sample, the model first produces visual and textual predictions, then estimates modality reliability from running anchors and cross-modality conflict, and finally regularizes the fusion gate toward the more reliable modality. The fused prediction is optimized with entropy minimization, gate regularization, and batch diversity. The rest of this section first states the practical adaptation rule used in deployment and then introduces the majorization-based mixing view that motivates it.

3.2. Idealized Multimodal Posterior Mixing

To analyze modality-specific shift, we introduce latent clean posteriors πv​(z)\pi^{v}(z) and πt​(z)\pi^{t}(z) for the two modalities, and a clean fused posterior πf​(z)∈ΔK−1\pi^{f}(z)\in\Delta^{K-1}. We model each shifted modality posterior as a mixed version of its clean counterpart.

Definition 3.0 (Doubly stochastic mixing).

A matrix D∈ℝK×KD\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} is doubly stochastic if Di​j≥0D_{ij}\geq 0 for all i,ji,j, each row sums to one, and each column sums to one. For a sample zz, the shifted posterior of modality m∈{v,t}m\in\{v,t\} follows

(5) pm​(z)=Dm​(z)​πm​(z)+rm​(z),p^{m}(z)=D^{m}(z)\pi^{m}(z)+r^{m}(z),

where Dm​(z)D^{m}(z) is doubly stochastic and rm​(z)r^{m}(z) is a residual term that measures deviation from ideal mixing.

When rm​(z)=0r^{m}(z)=0, the operator Dm​(z)D^{m}(z) redistributes probability mass without changing the total mass globally, which makes it a natural model for posterior flattening. Modality asymmetry arises because the two modalities may undergo different mixing operators, Dv​(z)D^{v}(z) and Dt​(z)D^{t}(z).

For analysis, we define the clean fusion target

(6) πf​(z)=β⋆​(z)​πv​(z)+(1−β⋆​(z))​πt​(z),\pi^{f}(z)=\beta^{\star}(z)\pi^{v}(z)+\bigl(1-\beta^{\star}(z)\bigr)\pi^{t}(z),

where β⋆​(z)∈[0,1]\beta^{\star}(z)\in[0,1] denotes the desired clean modality weight.

Proposition 3.1 (Entropy increase under ideal mixing).

Let u∈ΔK−1u\in\Delta^{K-1} and let DD be a doubly stochastic matrix. Then u⪰D​uu\succeq Du, where ⪰\succeq denotes majorization. Consequently, H⁡(D​u)≥H⁡(u)H(Du)\geq H(u).

Proposition 3.1 gives the basic direction of degradation: under ideal mixing, a shifted posterior becomes more mixed than its clean counterpart. This idealized view is used only for analysis. In deployment, we do not estimate the sample-wise mixing operator online; instead, we build a practical reliability signal from running modality anchors.

3.3. Reliability-Aware Gate Prior

The ideal analysis object is a modality-wise residual that measures how well the current posterior can be explained as a doubly stochastic mixing of a clean anchor. Let π¯m\bar{\pi}^{m} denote a clean modality anchor for modality m∈{v,t}m\in\{v,t\}. We define

(7) ρm⋆​(z)=minD∈𝒟K⁡‖pm​(z)−D​π¯m‖1,\rho^{\star}_{m}(z)=\min_{D\in\mathcal{D}_{K}}\left\|p^{m}(z)-D\bar{\pi}^{m}\right\|_{1},

where 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K} is the set of all K×KK\times K doubly stochastic matrices. A small value of ρm⋆​(z)\rho^{\star}_{m}(z) means that the current posterior remains well explained by a mixed clean anchor.

At test time, however, neither the clean anchor nor the optimal mixing operator is available. We therefore maintain a running anchor posterior p¯m\bar{p}^{m} for each modality and use a computable proxy

(8) ρ~m​(z)=‖sort↓⁡(pm​(z))−sort↓⁡(p¯m)‖1.\tilde{\rho}_{m}(z)=\left\|\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(p^{m}(z)\bigr)-\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(\bar{p}^{m}\bigr)\right\|_{1}.

The proxy is small when the current modality posterior remains close to its anchor and large when it drifts away. We compare sorted posterior profiles because majorization is characterized by ordered partial sums, so the proxy preserves the geometry most relevant to the analysis.

The running anchor is updated from recent high-confidence samples within the current batch. Let

(9) ℬmconf={z∈ℬ:maxk⁡pkm​(z)≥η},\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}_{m}=\{z\in\mathcal{B}:\max_{k}p^{m}_{k}(z)\geq\eta\},

(11) p¯m←μ​p¯m+(1−μ)​p^m,\bar{p}^{m}\leftarrow\mu\bar{p}^{m}+(1-\mu)\hat{p}^{m},

with μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) denoting the EMA momentum.

(12) κ⁡(z)=JS⁡(pv​(z),pt​(z))+λr​R​(pv​(z),pt​(z)),\kappa(z)=\operatorname{JS}\bigl(p^{v}(z),p^{t}(z)\bigr)+\lambda_{r}R\bigl(p^{v}(z),p^{t}(z)\bigr),

where JS⁡(⋅,⋅)\operatorname{JS}(\cdot,\cdot) is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (Lin, 1991) and R⁡(⋅,⋅)R(\cdot,\cdot) is a normalized ranking disagreement score.

(13) ℓv​(z)=−τ​ρ~v​(z),\ell^{v}(z)=-\tau\tilde{\rho}_{v}(z),
(14) ℓt​(z)=−τ​ρ~t​(z),\ell^{t}(z)=-\tau\tilde{\rho}_{t}(z),

(16) ℓv​(z)←ℓv​(z)−λc​κ​(z)​d​(z),\ell^{v}(z)\leftarrow\ell^{v}(z)-\lambda_{c}\kappa(z)\,d(z),
(17) ℓt​(z)←ℓt​(z)+λc​κ​(z)​d​(z),\ell^{t}(z)\leftarrow\ell^{t}(z)+\lambda_{c}\kappa(z)\,d(z),

where λc≥0\lambda_{c}\geq 0 controls the strength of the conflict correction. The resulting modality prior is

(18) [av​(z),at​(z)]=softmax⁡(ℓv​(z),ℓt​(z)).[a^{v}(z),a^{t}(z)]=\operatorname{softmax}\bigl(\ell^{v}(z),\ell^{t}(z)\bigr).

This asymmetric correction is necessary: adding the same conflict offset to both logits would cancel under the softmax and would not affect the gate prior.

3.4. Majorization-Aware Adaptation Objective

The three terms in Eq. (4) are

(19) ℒent​(ϕ)=1|ℬ|​∑z∈ℬH⁡(qϕ​(z)),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}(\phi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{B}}H\bigl(q_{\phi}(z)\bigr),
(20) ℒgate(ϕ)=1|ℬ|∑z∈ℬKL([αϕ(z),1−αϕ(z)]∥[av(z),at(z)]),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gate}}(\phi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{B}}\operatorname{KL}\Bigl([\alpha_{\phi}(z),1-\alpha_{\phi}(z)]\,\big\|\,[a^{v}(z),a^{t}(z)]\Bigr),
(21) ℒdiv​(ϕ)=−H⁡(1|ℬ|​∑z∈ℬqϕ​(z)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{div}}(\phi)=-H\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{B}}q_{\phi}(z)\right).

The entropy term sharpens the fused posterior. The gate term regularizes the learned fusion weight toward the reliability-aware prior in Eq. (18). The diversity term discourages the batch marginal from collapsing to a single class. Only the lightweight gate or adapter is updated throughout test-time adaptation.

3.5. Theoretical Analysis in the Main Text

We now state the main results that connect the idealized mixing model in Sec. 3.2 to the practical gate prior in Sec. 3.3. Proofs are deferred to the appendix.

Definition 3.1 (Top-one margin).

For a clean fused posterior πf​(z)\pi^{f}(z), let c⋆​(z)=argmaxkπkf​(z)c^{\star}(z)=\argmax_{k}\pi^{f}_{k}(z). The clean top-one margin is

(22) γ⁡(z)=πc⋆​(z)f​(z)−maxj≠c⋆​(z)⁡πjf​(z).\gamma(z)=\pi^{f}_{c^{\star}(z)}(z)-\max_{j\neq c^{\star}(z)}\pi^{f}_{j}(z).

The sample is margin-separable if γ⁡(z)>0\gamma(z)>0.

Theorem 3 (Sufficient condition for beneficial demixing).

Fix a sample zz with margin-separable clean fused posterior πf​(z)\pi^{f}(z). Assume that the adapted fused posterior qϕ​(z)q_{\phi}(z) satisfies three conditions: (i) qϕ​(z)⪰pf​(z)q_{\phi}(z)\succeq p^{f}(z); (ii) the order of the largest two coordinates of qϕ​(z)q_{\phi}(z) agrees with that of πf​(z)\pi^{f}(z); and (iii) ‖qϕ​(z)−πf​(z)‖∞<γ⁡(z)/2\|q_{\phi}(z)-\pi^{f}(z)\|_{\infty}<\gamma(z)/2. Then

(23) H⁡(qϕ​(z))≤H⁡(pf​(z))H\bigl(q_{\phi}(z)\bigr)\leq H\bigl(p^{f}(z)\bigr)

and

(24) argmaxkqϕ,k​(z)=c⋆​(z).\argmax_{k}q_{\phi,k}(z)=c^{\star}(z).

Theorem 3 separates two requirements that entropy alone does not capture. The majorization condition gives a valid demixing direction, while the ranking and margin conditions prevent an incorrect class from overtaking the clean top class. Entropy reduction is beneficial only when both requirements hold.

Corollary 3.2 (Correctness transfer from the clean fused classifier).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3, if the clean fused classifier predicts the true label of sample zz, then the adapted fused classifier also predicts the true label of sample zz.

The next result identifies a concrete failure regime caused by biased modality weighting.

Proposition 3.3 (Failure threshold under modality dominance).

Fix a sample zz and let cc denote the correct class. Let jj be any competing class. Define the modality-specific margins

(25) Δc,jv​(z)=pcv​(z)−pjv​(z),Δc,jt​(z)=pct​(z)−pjt​(z).\Delta^{v}_{c,j}(z)=p^{v}_{c}(z)-p^{v}_{j}(z),\qquad\Delta^{t}_{c,j}(z)=p^{t}_{c}(z)-p^{t}_{j}(z).

Assume that Δc,jv​(z)<0<Δc,jt​(z)\Delta^{v}_{c,j}(z)<0<\Delta^{t}_{c,j}(z). For the convex fusion rule in Eq. (3), if

(26) αϕ​(z)>Δc,jt​(z)Δc,jt​(z)−Δc,jv​(z),\alpha_{\phi}(z)>\frac{\Delta^{t}_{c,j}(z)}{\Delta^{t}_{c,j}(z)-\Delta^{v}_{c,j}(z)},

then qϕ,c​(z)<qϕ,j​(z)q_{\phi,c}(z)<q_{\phi,j}(z). In other words, if the gate places too much weight on the visually biased modality, the fused decision must flip to the wrong class.

Proposition 3.3 explains why entropy minimization alone is insufficient in the multimodal setting. When one modality favors the correct class and the other favors a competing class, crossing the threshold in Eq. (26) guarantees a ranking reversal in the fused posterior.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Setup

We evaluate MG-MTTA under three test regimes: visual shift, semantics-preserving textual shift, and joint shift. The visual setting serves to anchor the method to standard corruption benchmarks, while the textual and joint settings more directly test the multimodal fusion failures that motivate this paper. We further use diagnostic analyses and failure cases to examine whether the observed behavior is consistent with the proposed majorization-based view.

4.1.1. Benchmarks and shift construction.

All main-text experiments are instantiated under a shared ImageNet label space, which allows visual, textual, and joint shift to be compared within a single protocol.

Visual robustness is evaluated on CIFAR-100C and ImageNet-C from the common-corruptions benchmark family (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019). Unless otherwise stated, we report mean top-1 accuracy over the 15 corruption types at severity level 5. This part mainly serves as a benchmark-anchoring comparison to existing CLIP test-time adaptation results.

The textual setting is constructed differently. We keep the image fixed and perturb only the prompt bank, while preserving class identity. The L1–L4 ladder is not built from arbitrary prompt rewrites. Instead, it is motivated by the input-processing mechanism of CLIP-style text encoders, whose representations are sensitive to token boundaries, character-level perturbations, and local prompt context. We therefore apply label-preserving token- and context-level perturbations that progressively destabilize the text representation without changing the underlying class semantics. The resulting perturbations include prompt-template drift, lexical substitution, and removal of non-essential modifiers, and are averaged into a unified textual-shift score over the same ImageNet label space.

Joint shift combines image corruption with the semantics-preserving textual perturbations above. By contrast, prompt perturbations that conflict with class semantics—such as negation, incorrect attributes, or class-inconsistent descriptions—are excluded from the main benchmark and reserved for failure analysis, because they probe the modality-dominance mechanism in Sec. 3.5 more directly than the main robustness protocol does. This separation keeps the visual benchmark comparable to prior work, while using the textual and joint settings to test whether adaptation can recover reliable multimodal fusion under asymmetric shift. Full perturbation rules and additional protocol details are deferred to Appendix F.

4.1.2. Compared methods.

Our comparisons are organized around two baseline groups. The main comparisons in the textual and joint settings use matched internal baselines, so that backbone, prompt bank, update scope, and adaptation budget remain fixed across methods. In this group, Source-only evaluates the frozen vision-language backbone without test-time adaptation. Entropy-only updates the same parameter subset as MG-MTTA but optimizes only fused-posterior entropy. Entropy + Diversity adds the diversity regularizer on top of fused entropy minimization. These baselines are compared against MG-MTTA, which uses fused entropy minimization together with proxy-guided gate regularization and diversity regularization.

We also report representative external CLIP test-time adaptation baselines in the visual-shift setting, including TENT-Visual (Wang et al., 2020), SAR (Niu et al., 2023), TPT (Shu et al., 2022b), VTE (Döbler et al., 2024), and BATCLIP (Maharana et al., 2024). These methods were primarily introduced for visual corruption or prompt adaptation benchmarks, so we use them only in the visual comparison. For textual and joint shift, we restrict the comparison to the matched internal baselines in order to keep the multimodal evaluation protocol controlled and directly comparable.

4.1.3. Implementation and fairness protocol.

All main-text experiments use CLIP ViT-B/16 as the primary vision-language backbone (Radford et al., 2021). Unless noted otherwise, both modality encoders are frozen. Adaptation updates are restricted to a lightweight gate or adapter module and, when enabled, normalization-related parameters selected by name pattern. In implementation, fusion is performed at the logit level:

(27) zfuse​(z)=αϕ​(z)​zv​(z)+(1−αϕ​(z))​zt​(z),z_{\mathrm{fuse}}(z)=\alpha_{\phi}(z)z_{v}(z)+\bigl(1-\alpha_{\phi}(z)\bigr)z_{t}(z),

followed by

(28) qϕ​(z)=softmax⁡(zfuse​(z)).q_{\phi}(z)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\bigl(z_{\mathrm{fuse}}(z)\bigr).

All main-text results are obtained under episodic test-time adaptation, meaning that the model state is reset for each target-shift condition. Across methods, we keep the class vocabulary, clean and shifted prompt banks, and target ordering fixed. Unless a baseline explicitly requires otherwise, we also use the same optimizer family and the same adaptation-step budget. Hyperparameter search details and prompt examples are provided in Appendix F–H. Results on ViT-B/32 are reported separately in Appendix L.

4.2. Main Results

4.2.1. Visual-shift anchoring results.

We begin with the visual-only benchmark to position MG-MTTA relative to standard CLIP test-time adaptation results. This setting is included primarily as a benchmark-anchoring comparison rather than as the main test of multimodal fusion.

Table 1 reports the visual-shift results on CIFAR-100C and ImageNet-C. To keep the main text compact, we report only the mean top-1 accuracy over the 15 corruption types at severity level 5. Detailed corruption-wise results are provided in Appendix F.1 in Table 6.

On visual-only corruption, MG-MTTA remains aligned with the matched entropy-based internal baselines under the same lightweight adaptation protocol. This result anchors the method on standard CLIP corruption benchmarks. The stronger separation appears in the textual and joint regimes, where modality-specific perturbations directly affect fusion and reliability-aware adaptation becomes central.

4.2.2. Main multimodal results.

We next turn to the central setting of this paper: multimodal test-time adaptation under semantics-preserving textual shift and joint shift, where modality-specific perturbations affect fusion more directly than in the visual-only benchmark. Here we focus on the matched internal baselines so that all compared methods share the same backbone, prompt bank, update scope, and adaptation budget.

Table 2 reports the main multimodal results under textual shift and joint shift. The textual-shift column measures robustness to prompt-bank drift while holding the image fixed, whereas the joint-shift column evaluates the full modality-specific shift scenario studied in this paper. Of the two, the joint-shift regime is the more demanding one, since it tests whether adaptation can recover reliable fusion when both modalities are perturbed simultaneously.

Under semantics-preserving textual shift, Entropy-only and Entropy + Diversity both fall below Source-only. Lower fused entropy therefore does not by itself recover the correct multimodal decision when the text branch is perturbed. MG-MTTA instead improves over Source-only by +8.54 points.

Joint shift gives the harder multimodal test. When image corruption and textual perturbation are applied together, Entropy-only gives no gain over Source-only, and Entropy + Diversity improves by only +0.08 points. MG-MTTA improves by +4.59 points, indicating that reliability-aware adaptation is most useful when fusion is strained by asymmetric perturbations.

These results support the main empirical claim: lower fused entropy alone is not a sufficient criterion for multimodal test-time adaptation. The strongest gains appear in the textual and joint regimes, where asymmetric perturbations directly affect fusion. Level-wise results in Appendix F.2 and Table 7 show the same pattern across L1–L4 rather than at a single stress level. Under the L5 strongest probe, MG-MTTA improves over Source-only from 25.48 to 65.88 in the textual setting and from 9.66 to 26.13 in the joint setting; full diagnostics are reported in Appendix J. The textual/joint advantage also transfers to CLIP ViT-B/32, where MG-MTTA improves from 52.26 to 65.61 under textual shift and from 37.61 to 46.16 under joint shift; see Appendix L.

4.3. Mechanism Analysis

The analysis in Sec. 3.5 separates entropy reduction from reliable recovery: sharpening is useful only when the fused posterior moves along a valid de-mixing direction and preserves the decisive ranking. We therefore examine the main results through entropy–accuracy trajectories, majorization diagnostics, reliability signals, and collapse statistics.

Table 3 reports four diagnostics. The ranking-consistency ratios measure how often the clean posterior majorizes the shifted posterior and how often the adapted posterior majorizes the shifted posterior. Dist. to perm. measures proximity to permutation vertices of the simplex, separating de-mixing from brittle sharpening toward nearly one-hot predictions. Collapse measures batch-level concentration and flags degenerate class concentration during entropy minimization.

Is entropy reduction sufficient?

Fig. 3(a) compares entropy drop with accuracy gain across the L1–L4 textual ladder. Entropy-only can reduce entropy while giving little or negative accuracy gain. MG-MTTA shows a more stable relation between entropy decrease and accuracy improvement in both textual and joint settings. This agrees with the analysis: entropy reduction is helpful only when the update direction is constrained.

Does improvement align with de-mixing?

Fig. 3(b) relates accuracy gain to the majorization ratio. The gains of MG-MTTA are better aligned with de-mixing diagnostics than with entropy reduction alone. We use this relation as mechanism-level evidence, not as a standalone predictor of accuracy across all methods and settings.

Do reliability signals track modality stress?

Fig. 4 shows that both the reliability gap and cross-modality conflict increase as textual stress becomes stronger. The effect is more pronounced in the joint setting, where the visual branch is also corrupted. Since positive reliability gap values indicate that the text branch remains more anchor-consistent, the gate prior changes in the direction suggested by modality imbalance rather than applying a fixed heuristic correction.

Why is joint shift harder than textual shift?

The textual and joint settings differ in their diagnostic profile. Under textual shift, Dist. to perm. is very small and Collapse is zero, suggesting that the main difficulty is recovering a stable text-side signal. Under joint shift, Collapse is much larger even though the ranking-consistency ratio is not lower than in the textual case. Joint shift therefore introduces an additional fusion-fragility component: the posterior is not only degraded, but also more prone to brittle concentration when both streams are perturbed.

4.4. Ablation and Failure Analysis

L1–L4 form the calibrated textual benchmark used in the main results. L5 is kept separate as the strongest text-side stress probe: it applies more severe perturbation and is used for objective ablation and case-level failure analysis. We do not merge L5 into the main benchmark average.

Figure 5 shows three representative L5 cases: recovery from severe textual stress, a lower-entropy but still incorrect prediction, and recovery under high cross-modality conflict. These cases separate two outcomes that entropy alone cannot distinguish. In some samples, sharpening follows recovery; in others, it amplifies confidence in a wrong fused decision because the gate remains biased toward an unreliable modality.

Table 4 gives a compact stress-test ablation. Entropy-only falls below Source-only in both textual L5 and joint L5, and adding batch diversity alone does not recover the drop. MG-MTTA instead improves by +40.40 points under textual L5 and by +16.47 points under joint L5. The result isolates the main role of reliability-aware adaptation: under severe modality-specific shift, the fused posterior should not merely be sharpened, but sharpened along a reliability-consistent direction.

The complete L5 diagnostics, including majorization ratio and collapse statistics, are reported in Appendix J. Source-only severity calibration for the textual ladder is provided in Table 10, and additional failure cases are deferred to the appendix.

5. Limitations

MG-MTTA is designed for modality-specific shift, especially textual and joint regimes where asymmetric fusion errors dominate. On visual-only corruption benchmarks, it is competitive with matched entropy-based variants but not the strongest external CLIP adaptation baseline. The method relies on running anchors and a calibrated semantics-preserving textual stress protocol. Runtime and memory overhead are not separately quantified in this version, so efficiency claims are limited to the small trainable parameter subset.

6. Conclusion

This paper studies test-time adaptation for vision-language models under modality-specific shift. We formulate multimodal adaptation as a de-mixing problem on the fused posterior and show that entropy reduction alone is insufficient: it is useful only when the adapted posterior follows a valid majorization-consistent direction while preserving the decisive ranking. MG-MTTA implements this view by keeping the CLIP ViT-B/16 backbone frozen and adapting a lightweight gate or adapter with fused-posterior entropy minimization, reliability-aware gate regularization, and batch diversity. The diagnostics and failure cases are consistent with the proposed explanation: entropy-only adaptation may sharpen the wrong fused decision, whereas reliability-aware adaptation more often aligns entropy reduction with recovery. The main empirical advantage appears in textual and joint regimes, where asymmetric perturbations make multimodal fusion the core test-time adaptation challenge.

This appendix collects auxiliary definitions that are useful for proofs and implementation. The majorization relation u⪰vu\succeq v for u,v∈ΔK−1u,v\in\Delta^{K-1} means

(29) ∑i=1mu[i]≥∑i=1mv[i]for all ​m∈{1,…,K−1},\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{[i]}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{[i]}\quad\text{for all }m\in\{1,\dots,K-1\},

and equality holds automatically for m=Km=K because both vectors lie on the simplex. The ranking disagreement score in Eq. (12) may be instantiated as the normalized Kendall distance between the rankings induced by pv​(z)p^{v}(z) and pt​(z)p^{t}(z). The ideal quantity in Eq. (7) is introduced for analysis only. The deployed implementation instead uses the anchor-based proxy ρ~m​(z)\tilde{\rho}_{m}(z) described in Sec. 3.3 and Appendix F.

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 3.1

Let u∈ΔK−1u\in\Delta^{K-1} and let DD be doubly stochastic. By the Hardy Littlewood Polya theorem, a vector vv satisfies u⪰vu\succeq v if and only if there exists a doubly stochastic matrix DD such that v=D​uv=Du. Therefore u⪰D​uu\succeq Du. The Shannon entropy is Schur concave on the probability simplex. Hence u⪰D​uu\succeq Du implies H⁡(D​u)≥H⁡(u)H(Du)\geq H(u). This proves Proposition 3.1.

Appendix C Proof of Theorem 3

The first claim follows immediately from Condition 1 and the Schur concavity of Shannon entropy. Since qϕ​(z)⪰pf​(z)q_{\phi}(z)\succeq p^{f}(z), we obtain

(30) H⁡(qϕ​(z))≤H⁡(pf​(z)).H\bigl(q_{\phi}(z)\bigr)\leq H\bigl(p^{f}(z)\bigr).

It remains to prove the ranking statement. Let c⋆=c⋆​(z)=argmaxkπkf​(z)c^{\star}=c^{\star}(z)=\argmax_{k}\pi^{f}_{k}(z). For any class j≠c⋆j\neq c^{\star},

(31) qϕ,c⋆​(z)−qϕ,j​(z)=πc⋆f​(z)−πjf​(z)+(qϕ,c⋆​(z)−πc⋆f​(z))−(qϕ,j​(z)−πjf​(z)),q_{\phi,c^{\star}}(z)-q_{\phi,j}(z)=\pi^{f}_{c^{\star}}(z)-\pi^{f}_{j}(z)+\bigl(q_{\phi,c^{\star}}(z)-\pi^{f}_{c^{\star}}(z)\bigr)-\bigl(q_{\phi,j}(z)-\pi^{f}_{j}(z)\bigr),
(32) qϕ,c⋆​(z)−qϕ,j​(z)≥γ⁡(z)−2​‖qϕ​(z)−πf​(z)‖∞,q_{\phi,c^{\star}}(z)-q_{\phi,j}(z)\geq\gamma(z)-2\|q_{\phi}(z)-\pi^{f}(z)\|_{\infty},
(33) qϕ,c⋆​(z)−qϕ,j​(z)>0,q_{\phi,c^{\star}}(z)-q_{\phi,j}(z)>0,

where the last inequality uses Condition 3. Therefore qϕ,c⋆​(z)>qϕ,j​(z)q_{\phi,c^{\star}}(z)>q_{\phi,j}(z) for all j≠c⋆j\neq c^{\star}, which implies argmaxkqϕ,k​(z)=c⋆\argmax_{k}q_{\phi,k}(z)=c^{\star}. Condition 2 ensures that the decisive order of the largest coordinates is consistent with the clean fused posterior and rules out a tie induced by reordering near the top of the simplex. This completes the proof.

Appendix D Proof of Corollary 3.2

If the clean fused classifier predicts the true label, then the true label is equal to c⋆​(z)=argmaxkπkf​(z)c^{\star}(z)=\argmax_{k}\pi^{f}_{k}(z). By Theorem 3, the adapted fused classifier satisfies argmaxkqϕ,k​(z)=c⋆​(z)\argmax_{k}q_{\phi,k}(z)=c^{\star}(z). Hence it predicts the true label as well.

For a fixed competing class jj, the fused margin between the correct class cc and class jj is

Appendix F Implementation Details

Evaluation settings. Table 5 summarizes the evaluation settings used in the main paper.

Backbone and frozen components. We instantiate the main experiments with CLIP ViT-B/16 and keep both the visual encoder and the text encoder frozen throughout test-time adaptation unless a compared baseline explicitly requires encoder updates. The adaptation update is restricted to a lightweight parameter subset, which may be instantiated as a scalar gate, a small fusion adapter, or normalization-related parameters in the fusion block. This design matches the formulation in the main text, where the adapted fused posterior is controlled by a lightweight parameter set while the backbone remains fixed.

Adaptation protocol. Unless otherwise stated, the main results follow an episodic test-time adaptation protocol. That is, the adaptation state is reset for each target-shift condition. Additional online adaptation results may be reported separately when the target stream is treated as a continuous deployment sequence.

Optimization. All adaptation methods use the same optimizer family and the same target-stream ordering. The learning rate, weight decay, and the number of update steps per batch are chosen from the ranges listed in Table 8. The source model, entropy-based baselines, and MG-MTTA share the same frozen backbone, class vocabulary, and prompt bank so that differences are attributable to the adaptation rule rather than to backbone or prompt changes.

Prompt bank sharing. For every dataset, all compared methods use the same clean prompt bank and the same shifted prompt bank. No method is allowed to use a task-specific or method-specific prompt set. This protocol ensures that prompt variation is treated as part of the target shift rather than as an extra source of tuning freedom.

Reliability proxies. The main experiments do not solve the inner minimization in Eq. (7) online. Instead, each modality maintains a running anchor posterior p¯m\bar{p}^{m} from recent high-confidence samples, and MG-MTTA computes the practical reliability proxy

(38) ρ~m​(z)=‖sort↓⁡(pm​(z))−sort↓⁡(p¯m)‖1.\tilde{\rho}_{m}(z)=\left\|\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(p^{m}(z)\bigr)-\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(\bar{p}^{m}\bigr)\right\|_{1}.

This proxy is the implementation used throughout the main experiments, and it is the quantity that defines the gate prior in Eq. (18). The ideal residual ρm⋆​(z)\rho^{\star}_{m}(z) in Eq. (7) is retained only as an analysis object that motivates the modality-to-anchor structure of the practical method. We emphasize that the practical proxy is not introduced as a loose efficiency approximation to the ideal DS-fit quantity. Rather, it is a theory-guided practical instantiation: it preserves the modality-to-anchor reference, the sorted posterior geometry, and the relative reliability ordering required by the gate, while avoiding the cost and instability of solving a sample-wise doubly-stochastic optimization problem online.

Table 7 expands the main-text averages in Table 2 into level-wise results for textual and joint stress. This table checks that the gain of MG-MTTA is not concentrated on a single stress level. Appendix G Hyperparameter Ranges and Selection Protocol

Table 8 summarizes the candidate values screened in pilot runs and the final values used in the reported ImageNet/ImageNet-C experiments. Unless otherwise stated, the same final configuration is used for both textual and joint stress settings. For methods that do not use gated multimodal fusion (e.g., Source-only and Entropy-only baselines), gate-related coefficients are inactive and set to 00.

Selection protocol.

We use a two-stage selection procedure. First, candidate ranges are screened in pilot runs under representative shift conditions. Second, one final configuration is chosen using held-out performance and stability criteria, including lower variance across shift types and reduced batch-collapse tendency. No target labels are used inside the adaptation update loop.

Reported configuration.

For the reported main experiments, MG-MTTA uses lr=10−3\mathrm{lr}=10^{-3}, wd=0\mathrm{wd}=0, steps=2=2, λg=0.1\lambda_{g}=0.1, λd=0.01\lambda_{d}=0.01, λc=0.25\lambda_{c}=0.25, τ=5.0\tau=5.0, η=0.7\eta=0.7, and μ=0.9\mu=0.9. A small nonzero conflict-correction weight is selected in the reported configuration based on held-out performance and stability under textual and joint stress. Accordingly, the main results reflect the combined effect of the anchor-based reliability prior, gate regularization, explicit conflict correction, and entropy/diversity objectives.

Appendix H Prompt Construction and Textual Shift Protocol

Our textual-shift design is guided by the text-processing mechanism of CLIP-style vision–language models rather than by arbitrary prompt rewriting. In CLIP/OpenCLIP-style models, the text branch maps each prompt into a fixed-length token sequence and then into a single text representation used for image–text matching. This makes the model sensitive not only to prompt semantics, but also to token boundaries, character-level perturbations, and local prompt context. Motivated by this property, we construct a token-level textual stress protocol that perturbs the prompt in ways that remain largely label-preserving while progressively degrading the stability of the text representation.

The textual-shift protocol is divided into two categories.

Semantics-preserving textual stress.

This category is used in the main experiments. Its goal is not to change the class label, but to perturb the prompt at the token and local-context level in a controlled manner. Compared with purely semantic paraphrasing, this construction is more directly tied to how CLIP-style text encoders tokenize and represent prompts. Accordingly, the main protocol operates on token boundaries, character-level spelling noise, and mild context degradation while preserving the underlying class identity.

We instantiate a five-level token-level textual stress ladder:

  • •

    L1: context-only typo. Mild character-level perturbation is applied to prompt-context words such as photo, image, or picture, without modifying the class phrase itself.

  • •

    L2: context typo + class-boundary perturbation. In addition to the L1 context perturbation, the class phrase is modified at the boundary level, for example by replacing spaces with hyphens or underscores, while avoiding inner-token corruption.

  • •

    L3: partial mild class-token corruption. Based on L2, a deterministic subset of classes receives an additional mild inner-token perturbation on the class phrase. This increases difficulty while retaining approximate human readability.

  • •

    L4: expanded class-token corruption with mild context drop. Relative to L3, the subset of classes receiving class-token corruption is enlarged, and the local grammatical context is mildly degraded. This produces a stronger but still label-preserving prompt shift.

  • •

    L5: global mild class-token corruption. All classes receive prompt-context perturbation together with mild corruption of the class phrase. This defines the strongest level used in the main textual-stress benchmark.

The severity ladder is calibrated under the frozen source-only model. This calibration step is important because the goal of the textual-stress protocol is to define an input-side perturbation scale, rather than to encode the behavior of a particular adaptation method. In the appendix, we therefore report the clean-to-L5 accuracy trend under the source-only model as an explicit severity check.

Conflicting textual shift.

This category is used only in failure analysis and is not part of the main robustness comparison. Unlike the semantics-preserving protocol above, these perturbations may alter or conflict with the class semantics and are therefore reserved for studying failure modes such as harmful confidence amplification and modality-dominance errors. The allowed operations include:

  • •

    negation,

  • •

    incorrect attributes,

  • •

    class-inconsistent descriptions.

Representative examples include:

  • •

    not a photo of a {class},

  • •

    a photo of a wrong-attribute {class},

  • •

    a photo of another class.

Reason for the separation.

The main comparison evaluates adaptation under controlled, label-preserving textual stress rather than under explicit semantic contradiction. Separating semantics-preserving stress from conflicting textual perturbations prevents the main benchmark from being confounded by prompts that directly alter the decision semantics. This separation also matches the theoretical narrative of the paper: the main protocol probes robustness under modality-specific but still semantically aligned shift, whereas the conflicting protocol is used to expose concrete failure regimes.

Appendix I Additional Metrics and Reliability Proxies

In addition to task accuracy, we record the following theory-aligned auxiliary measurements.

Entropy change.

For each sample, we record the entropy of the pre-adaptation fused posterior and the entropy of the adapted fused posterior. This quantity verifies that the deployed method is indeed performing entropy reduction, but it is not treated as sufficient evidence of successful adaptation on its own.

Majorization ratio.

For each shift setting, we compute the proportion of samples for which the adapted fused posterior majorizes the pre-adaptation fused posterior, as well as the proportion of samples for which the adapted fused posterior moves closer to a clean proxy posterior in sorted partial sums. This metric is the most direct operational counterpart of the majorization-based de-mixing view in the main text.

Anchor-based reliability proxy.

For each modality, we record the practical reliability quantity

(39) ρ~m​(z)=‖sort↓⁡(pm​(z))−sort↓⁡(p¯m)‖1,\tilde{\rho}_{m}(z)=\left\|\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(p^{m}(z)\bigr)-\operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow}\!\bigl(\bar{p}^{m}\bigr)\right\|_{1},

where p¯m\bar{p}^{m} is the running anchor posterior. Smaller values indicate better consistency with the modality anchor and hence higher estimated reliability. This is the practical reliability quantity used in the main experiments. It should not be interpreted as an exact solution of the ideal doubly stochastic residual in Eq. (7), but as a computable proxy that preserves the same modality-to-anchor structure and the sorted-profile geometry relevant to majorization.

Distance to permutation vertices.

To measure whether adaptation pushes the posterior toward an extreme but potentially brittle decision, we compute a proxy distance from the posterior to permutation vertices of the simplex. This quantity helps distinguish useful de-mixing from degenerate sharpening toward unstable one-hot decisions.

Cross-modality conflict.

We record the Jensen–Shannon divergence term, the ranking disagreement term, and the combined conflict score used in the gate prior. These quantities characterize how strongly the visual and textual branches disagree under modality-specific shift.

Collapse statistics.

At the batch level, we record the entropy of the batch marginal, class-frequency imbalance, and additional collapse indicators used in the implementation. These measurements are used to detect whether entropy reduction is accompanied by undesirable batch-level concentration.

Severity calibration for textual stress.

Because the main textual-shift protocol is motivated by tokenization-level and local-context perturbations in the CLIP-style text branch, we additionally report the clean-to-L5 performance trend under the frozen source-only model. This calibration is included to verify that the textual-stress ladder is monotonic and severity-ordered before any test-time adaptation is applied. In other words, the source-only calibration isolates the strength of the input-side textual perturbation itself, rather than conflating it with the behavior of a particular adaptation rule.

Appendix J Additional Ablation Settings

This appendix reports compact ablations beyond the calibrated main-text benchmark. The goal is not to repeat the L1–L4 results from the main paper, but to stress-test whether the proposed reliability-aware design remains effective under substantially stronger perturbations and whether the contribution of its components becomes more visible outside the moderate setting. Following the main paper, the visual appendix setting uses corruption severity level 5, while the textual appendix setting is instantiated with the L5 strongest textual probe. The joint strongest probe combines visual corruption at severity 5 with textual stress at L5.

The L5 textual condition is treated as a strongest probe rather than as a direct extension of the calibrated L1–L4 textual benchmark. Its role is to stress-test robustness under a substantially harder text-side perturbation, not to serve as a directly comparable continuation of the main textual ladder. This design is motivated by the text-processing mechanism of CLIP-style models, whose text encoder is sensitive to token boundaries, character-level perturbations, and local prompt context. Source-only severity calibration for this textual ladder is reported in Table 10.

We report two complementary views. First, a strongest-probe objective ablation compares matched entropy-based baselines and the full method under textual and joint L5 stress. Second, a compact three-mode ablation compares trainable-subset variants and objective variants across visual, textual strongest-probe, and joint settings.

Table 11 shows that MG-MTTA remains substantially stronger than the entropy-based baselines under both textual and joint L5 stress. In particular, the strongest textual probe remains highly favorable to MG-MTTA, indicating that the method remains effective not only under joint multimodal stress but also under severe text-only perturbation. At the same time, these strongest-probe results should not be interpreted as implying that any single diagnostic quantity explains performance on its own. In particular, the majorization ratio does not vary monotonically with accuracy across methods and settings. This behavior is consistent with the main-text claim that lower entropy, or any single posterior-sharpening statistic, is not by itself a sufficient indicator of successful multimodal adaptation under severe modality-specific shift.

We next compare both trainable-subset variants and objective variants in a compact three-mode stress test. The subset variants are: Gate only, which updates only the gate parameters; Adapter only, which updates only the adapter parameters; and Normalization only, which updates only normalization-related parameters. The objective variants are: Entropy + gate, which keeps the full trainable subset but removes the diversity term; Entropy + Diversity, which performs entropy-based adaptation without the reliability-aware gate prior; and MG-MTTA, the full method with the complete trainable subset and all objective terms enabled.

Table 12 compares lightweight update scopes and constrained-adaptation variants under the strongest probe. Under textual L5, the constrained variants form a near-tie around 65.8%, while Entropy + Diversity remains much lower at 22.18%. This indicates that the dominant factor under severe text-side stress is whether adaptation is constrained away from entropy-only sharpening, rather than which lightweight subset is uniquely updated.

Under joint L5, the full MG-MTTA objective gives the strongest result among the compared variants. The gain over other constrained variants is smaller than the gap to Entropy + Diversity, so we interpret it as evidence of robustness under joint stress rather than as a strict ranking of update scopes. The visual-only column shows small differences across variants, consistent with its role as a benchmark anchor rather than the primary test of asymmetric multimodal fusion.

Appendix K Additional Failure Analysis

This appendix expands the case-wise analysis in Fig. 5 by providing a compact quantitative summary for three representative strongest-probe cases. These examples describe when entropy reduction is helpful and when it is not under severe textual and joint stress.

Case selection.

We consider three representative cases from the strongest-probe setting. Case A is a textual-L5 recovery case in which the frozen source-only prediction is incorrect but MG-MTTA restores the correct class. Case B is a joint-L5 failure case in which the fused-posterior entropy decreases slightly after adaptation, yet the final prediction remains incorrect. Case C is a joint-L5 recovery case in which MG-MTTA corrects an incorrect source-only prediction under strong cross-modality disagreement.

Interpretation.

Table 13 supports the same qualitative message as the main-text case analysis. Cases A and C show that MG-MTTA can recover from incorrect source-only predictions under severe textual or joint stress. By contrast, Case B shows that a decrease in fused-posterior entropy alone is not sufficient for successful multimodal adaptation. These examples should therefore be interpreted as compact case-level evidence complementary to Fig. 5, rather than as a standalone mechanistic verification.

Appendix L Additional Backbone Generalization

To examine whether the main empirical pattern observed in the main text is preserved beyond the primary backbone, we further evaluate the method on an additional CLIP variant. Since the goal of this experiment is to check cross-backbone consistency rather than to conduct a large-scale backbone study, we report a compact comparison on the main visual, textual, and joint settings.

Table 14 summarizes the additional backbone results. We compare the same matched internal baselines under visual shift, semantics-preserving textual shift, and joint shift. The visual column reports mean corruption accuracy, while the textual and joint columns follow the same evaluation protocol as in the main paper.

These results preserve the main multimodal pattern on an additional CLIP backbone. On ViT-B/32, the gains of MG-MTTA are concentrated in textual and joint shift, where it remains substantially stronger than the matched entropy-based baselines. The visual-only column is not the main target of this backbone check; it serves as the same corruption anchor used in the primary experiments.
